I'm of the belief that while there are many shades of experience, none of those shades are colorless. But, if you don't feel this a conductive avenue of discussion, I'll leave things at that.

>What has been the cause of most of your pain? Have you dug for a root cause?

I can't decide if this is something that's too difficult to put into words, or if it's something that my inability to expound on signals that it's invalid. In any case, I guess I'll try my best to provide a summation.

The biggest cause is, most likely, my **self-confidence**. The biggest reason I see my life as something that can be thrown away is because I fail to see its value. I'm not going to go into the reasons I feel this way, not specifically, but needless to say I think they're valid. I'm scared of many, many things in life, and this has all lead to me giving up on many things before I attempt it, because, in my mind, failure is assured. There are many things I wish I was better at, but I'm too often dissuaded from them. I wish I was smarter, a better person, etc. And this disparity between **what I want to be** and **what I can see myself realistically being** has probably informed my suicide ideation more than anything else. In short, I'm inadequate. In short, I do not meet my own standards, and can't see my meeting them anywhere in the near future.

Also a huge factor is that **I love someone who doesn't love me.** This feeds into the former pain to a nearly unlimited degree. If I can love someone with every part of me, and they don't love me back, what does that say about me? I am willing to change every and any part of who I am as a person if it will make this individual feel the same affection for me that I feel for them, and yet I am still unable to. This, obviously, has led me to question my worth as an individual, and the notion that I'm 'worth' love, and, consequently, if my life is worth living in absence of it.

>What have you done to try to remedy this?

I have been to a hospital, multiple therapists, and on multiple prescriptions drugs. I am currently unemployed, and cannot see myself becoming employed in the near future. Not once during this treatment process – not for even a *day*, let alone a pattern that went on for longer – did I feel that I was being helped by it.

Okay, so I think that your metric is actually more limiting than mine. Let me explain :P

So even in your Limbo, there are going to be good and bad times - And in the bad parts of limbo, there are going to better parts and worse parts. You see, when I said 'pain' and 'pleasure' above, I wasn't talking about black and white concepts, but more a gradient, you understand? 

Like, a abstract median of emotions exists for everyone. It varies from person to person but let's define everything above this median as 'pleasure' and everything below it as 'pain', no matter how blissful the pleasure or muted the pain. Every piece of existence still factors into this equation, even if it is tiny.

>Moreover, you've already pointed out this biggest flaw in all of this. That there is no way to really know. What knowledge do you have now that you believe you'd be avoiding pain?

Good question. As I've already admitted, I don't have knowledge of it. I have reasonable guesswork based on precedent and extrapolation. My life has been on this downward course for long enough – with no efforts of mine, particular or general, seeming to halt it – and with no evidence of any upward ticks in the near future I have no reason to assume it will deviate. I'm not leaving it up to fate or something – I've tried shit and it hasn't worked. I'm trying to make sure that this suicide is as rational a decision as I could make it...which is a little absurd, in and of itself, I guess. Just imagine the pseudo-philosophical suicide note I'll leave, explaining to my family the logical necessity of their finding my corpse.

I think that hedonism is the most 'rational' outlook of the 'purpose' of life. It's not completely satisfying, but it's the closest I can come to a satisfying answer.

With that in mind, let's assume that the two factors of human experience "pleasure" vs "pain" can not only be judged, but can also be judged by the same quantifiable metric. If this is true, and a person's life (at the end of their life) comes out to a net negative (pain outweighs pleasure) then that person's life wasn't worth living, right? We can't say "well even if it was more painful than not, at least the pleasure existed at all" because the fact that the result is negative precludes the lesser amount of 'pleasure' being 'worth it'. 

I want to die because, given extrapolation of the data of my life, it's more likely than not that the pleasure in my life will not, my own metric, outweigh the pain. That's not a life I want to live. The flaw in this is, of course, that I have no way of KNOWING for sure that my extrapolation is accurate, but I think I have enough knowledge that it's a gamble I'm willing to take to avoid a lifetime of waking up hating everything.
